senses.d: Good-for-nothing; not dependable.
ex: Bill never mows the lawn, takes out the trash or anything. He's useless, but I love him anyways.

Middle English usen English use Inherited from Middle English usen, from Old French user (“use, employ, practice”), from Medieval Latin usare (“use”), frequentative form of past participle stem of Latin uti (“to use”). Displaced native Middle English noten, nutten (“to use”) (from Old English notian, nēotan, nyttian) and Middle English brouken, bruken (“to use, enjoy”) (from Old English brūcan).

senses.d: The act of using.
ex: The use of torture has been condemned by the United Nations.

senses.d: The act of consuming alcohol or narcotics.
ex: Heavy alcohol use (2.5 drinks per day or more) at any age is unhealthy and should be avoided.

senses.d: Usefulness, utility, benefit; purpose, point.
ex: Near-synonyms: meaning, meaningfulness
What's the use of a law that nobody follows?

senses.d: A function; a purpose for which something may be employed.
ex: This tool has many uses.

senses.d: Occasion or need to employ; necessity.
ex: I have no further use for these textbooks, but we may have use for all these other things later.

senses.d: Interest for lent money; premium paid for the use of something; usury.
ex: Thou art more obliged to pay duty and tribute, use and principal, to him.

senses.d: Continued or repeated practice; usage; habit.
ex: Let later age that noble vse enuie,
How weary, stale, flat and unprofitable, / Seem to me all the uses of this world!

senses.d: Common occurrence; ordinary experience.
ex: O Caesar! these things are beyond all use.

senses.d: A special form of a rite adopted for use in a particular context, often a diocese.
ex: the Sarum, or Canterbury, use; the York use; the Ordinariate use
From henceforth all the whole realm shall have but one use.

senses.d: A slab of iron welded to the side of a forging, such as a shaft, near the end, and afterward drawn down, by hammering, so as to lengthen the forging.
To employ; to apply; to utilize.
ex: Use this knife to slice the bread.
We can use this mathematical formula to solve the problem.

senses.d: To expend; to consume by employing.
ex: I used the money they allotted me.
We should use up most of the fuel.

senses.d: To exploit.
ex: You never cared about me; you just used me!

senses.d: To consume (alcohol, drugs, etc), especially regularly.
ex: He uses cocaine.
I have never used drugs.

senses.d: To consume a previously specified substance, especially a drug to which one is addicted.
ex: Richard began experimenting with cocaine last year; now he uses almost every day.

senses.d: To benefit from; to be able to employ or stand.
ex: I could use a drink.
My car could use a new coat of paint.

senses.d: To suggest or request that other people employ a specific set of gender pronouns when referring to the subject.
ex: I use they/them pronouns.

senses.d: To accustom; to habituate. (Now common only in participial form. Uses the same pronunciation as the noun; see usage notes.)
ex: soldiers who are used to hardships and danger
to use the soldiers to hardships and danger

senses.d: To accustom oneself.
ex: We are not long in using ourselves to changes in life.

senses.d: To habitually do; to be wont to do. (Now chiefly in past-tense forms; see used to.)
ex: I used to get things done.
Use hospitality one to another without grudging.
